statement: A running track has two straight sections, each $90$ meters long, joined at their ends by two semicircles. Along the inside edge of the track, each semicircle has radius $30$ meters. Jada runs one lap along a path that stays exactly $2$ meters outside the inside edge all the way around. How many meters farther does she run than someone who runs one lap exactly along the inside edge?

choices.misconception: I thought running 2 m farther out adds just 2 m at each curved end, so I got 2 + 2 = 4.
I added the 2 m to the diameter of the curves instead of to the radius, so the circumference grew by only $2\pi$.
I thought the straight sections also got 2 m longer each, so I added 4 to the $4\pi$ from the curves.
I added 2 m to the radius once for each side of the track, so I made the radius 4 m bigger and got $2\pi \cdot 4 = 8\pi$.

hints: Which parts of Jada's lap are longer than the inside lap, and which are the same?
The straight sections are the same length for both runners. On the curves, Jada runs on semicircles of radius $32$ instead of $30$.
The two semicircles together make a full circle. Compare $2\pi \cdot 32$ with $2\pi \cdot 30$.

solutions.reliable: The straight sections are $90$ m for both runners. The inside lap's two semicircles together make one circle of radius $30$, length $2\pi \cdot 30 = 60\pi$. Jada's curves are semicircles of radius $32$, which together make a circle of length $2\pi \cdot 32 = 64\pi$. So she runs $64\pi - 60\pi = 4\pi$ meters farther, about $12.6$ m.
solutions.elegant: Only the curves change, and together they make one full circle. A circle's circumference grows by $2\pi$ for every meter added to its radius, so moving out $2$ m adds $2\pi \cdot 2 = 4\pi$, no matter how long the straights are or how big the curves are.
